title: Proxy
summary: Put a stand-in in front of an object to control access, laziness, or remote calls.

parts.rule: A proxy stands in for a real subject under the same interface and decides whether or when the real operation is reached. A virtual proxy delays expensive creation, a protection proxy checks access, and a remote proxy turns a local-looking call into network I/O. The proxy controls access; it does not translate to a different client interface.
parts.why: Lazy loading, authorization, and RPC mechanics become inconsistent when every caller implements them. A proxy puts that policy at one access point. The same interface can also hide important differences—especially latency and failure—so callers still need an honest contract for operations that may block or fail remotely.
parts.example: A gallery shows metadata for 100 photos, each backed by a 20 MB image. Photo exposes dimensions() and display(). HighResPhoto loads and decodes the file in its constructor. Creating 100 real objects would read about 2 GB even if the user opens one photo. PhotoProxy stores path and dimensions from cheap metadata. dimensions() returns immediately. On the first display() for photo 17, the proxy creates one HighResPhoto, pays the 20 MB load, and forwards display(); later calls reuse that instance. If two threads can call display() together, initialization must be synchronized so the file is not decoded twice. A protection proxy for Document.view(user) performs an ACL check before calling RealDocument.view, and returns Forbidden without constructing the document when access fails. A ShippingPortProxy may serialize quote(parcel) over HTTP, but its interface must expose or map timeout, unavailable, and retryable errors; a 2-second network call is not semantically identical to an in-memory calculation just because method names match. Decorator would wrap display() to add metrics or borders after access is granted. Adapter would rename or reshape a vendor method. Proxy answers a different question: may the caller reach the subject now?
parts.use: Use a proxy when access itself needs policy: defer a heavy object, enforce authorization, represent a remote service, or share one controlled reference. Keep the same subject contract, make hidden cost observable, and define caching, thread safety, timeout, and error behavior for the chosen proxy type.
parts.refuse: Do not pretend an unreliable remote call is a free local getter. Avoid proxy chains that make it unclear which layer denied or failed a call. If the wrapper adds optional responsibilities, consider decorator; if it changes interfaces, consider adapter. A direct reference is clearer when creation is cheap and every caller has the same access rights.

body:
Rule. A proxy stands in for a real subject under the same interface and decides whether or when the real operation is reached. A virtual proxy delays expensive creation, a protection proxy checks access, and a remote proxy turns a local-looking call into network I/O. The proxy controls access; it does not translate to a different client interface.

Why it matters. Lazy loading, authorization, and RPC mechanics become inconsistent when every caller implements them. A proxy puts that policy at one access point. The same interface can also hide important differences—especially latency and failure—so callers still need an honest contract for operations that may block or fail remotely.

Worked example. A gallery shows metadata for 100 photos, each backed by a 20 MB image. Photo exposes dimensions() and display(). HighResPhoto loads and decodes the file in its constructor. Creating 100 real objects would read about 2 GB even if the user opens one photo. PhotoProxy stores path and dimensions from cheap metadata. dimensions() returns immediately. On the first display() for photo 17, the proxy creates one HighResPhoto, pays the 20 MB load, and forwards display(); later calls reuse that instance. If two threads can call display() together, initialization must be synchronized so the file is not decoded twice. A protection proxy for Document.view(user) performs an ACL check before calling RealDocument.view, and returns Forbidden without constructing the document when access fails. A ShippingPortProxy may serialize quote(parcel) over HTTP, but its interface must expose or map timeout, unavailable, and retryable errors; a 2-second network call is not semantically identical to an in-memory calculation just because method names match. Decorator would wrap display() to add metrics or borders after access is granted. Adapter would rename or reshape a vendor method. Proxy answers a different question: may the caller reach the subject now?

[[diagram:proxy]]

When to use. Use a proxy when access itself needs policy: defer a heavy object, enforce authorization, represent a remote service, or share one controlled reference. Keep the same subject contract, make hidden cost observable, and define caching, thread safety, timeout, and error behavior for the chosen proxy type.

When to refuse. Do not pretend an unreliable remote call is a free local getter. Avoid proxy chains that make it unclear which layer denied or failed a call. If the wrapper adds optional responsibilities, consider decorator; if it changes interfaces, consider adapter. A direct reference is clearer when creation is cheap and every caller has the same access rights.
